title: iADD: Improving Alignment and Diversity in Diffusion Policy Optimization

paper.title: iADD: Improving Alignment and Diversity in Diffusion Policy Optimization
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning based post training of diffusion models, such as Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO), optimizes a reverse diffusion process under a reward function. However, current approaches to reward optimizations do so at the cost of diversity and quality. In this paper, we provide better tradeoffs through careful theoretical considerations and method design. We analyze the theoretical framework and mathematically demonstrate that only-latter timestep updates of diffusion model may be harmful for diversity contrary to the conclusions presented in a previous work. Additionally, we propose an incremental Feynman-Kac training based on strong theoretical foundations in order to achieve the best-yet alignment-diversity tradeoffs. We perform extensive experiments and compare our method against related diffusion policy optimization approaches in three different tasks and also provide strong ablations for each component, thus validating strong performance gains in both alignment and diversity. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion Models are currently the gold standard for generation and editing tasks on images [ 23 , 63 , 38 , 53 , 64 , 62 , 44 , 54 ] , videos [ 24 , 22 , 5 ] as well as 3D scenes [ 17 , 26 , 65 ] or objects. Through time-dependent iterative movement defining a path, diffusion methods learn to reach the target data distribution, exhibiting strong generalization and diversity [ 13 , 35 , 44 ] . Nevertheless, the quality of the modeling is limited by the target distribution samples; thus in most cases generation quality is naturally impacted for rare classes and specific user constraints. Reinforcement Learning (RL) [ 68 , 56 , 45 , 55 ] has the potential to address the problem, without using additional data, in the ideals of learning solely through experience [ 57 ] . Recent works [ 4 , 14 , 74 , 28 , 49 , 72 , 69 ] have precisely addressed the problem of finetuning the reverse diffusion process online, by applying the RL algorithm [ 68 ] . However, naive policy optimization of diffusion models can lead to mode collapse and general quality degradation of the generated samples [ 14 , 28 ] . This is reflected in the alignment-diversity tradeoffs , see Fig. 1 . Circumventing mode collapse and general quality degradation in lack of additional preference data [ 66 , 34 , 73 , 32 ] , though important is highly challenging. Thus, most approaches tend to be domain specific, and thus are validated on specific tasks. A more generic and theoretically grounded study of the alignment-diversity tradeoffs under the constraints of additional preference data-free rewards, remains under-explored. Existing solutions often perform regularization, e.g . through selected timestep updates [ 2 , 28 ] or via measuring the KL divergence [ 14 ] . Specifically, [ 28 ] intuitively argues that reward backpropagation is more reliable for latter timesteps and thus do not update the model on earlier timesteps. On the other hand, [ 2 , 41 ] refine middle timesteps based on the observation of how semantics are constructed in diffusion models [ 13 , 7 ] . Similarly, [ 14 , 74 ] specifically consider the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) in order to propose reward optimization strategies. Furthermore, [ 74 ] proposes a continuous time formulation in DDPM for RL policy optimization. In this paper, we study the alignment-diversity tradeoff in finetuning discrete-time denoising diffusion model through early intervention as well as careful regularization. We formulate the tradeoff problem as that of attaining the minimum change in the target samples required for the alignment, while preserving the original diversity through structural regularization, and target distribution’s volume preservation. We discover that attaining higher alignment with minimal diversity tradeoff requires early intervention via two processes. The first and retrospectively obvious solution is to update the early timesteps of the reverse denoising path, contrary to [ 28 ] that updates the late timesteps. We provide actionable theoretical results that untangles the puzzle of timestep selection. The results justify partial timestep selection from the viewpoint of target distribution’s volume preservation. Moreover, the theoretical analyses suggest an approach, which incrementally increases the per-iteration sparse timestep updates, over the course of the finetuning. Additionally, our second solution is to perform early intervention by looking ahead in the denoising path. Specifically, we propose the discrete-time implementation of the Feynman-Kac path guidance [ 11 , 33 , 58 , 60 , 61 , 30 ] during training in the following two ways: discontinuing least promising paths with low reward expectations to improve the alignment and branching the promising ones in order to encourage diversity. Table 1 shows the relative impact and relevant theory behind the method’s components. Figure 2 : Versatility across diverse generation tasks. Our final method, termed, iADD thus employs both early timestep update, early intervention as well as structural regularization in order to obtain a balanced approach to reward-based finetuning of diffusion models. We perform experiments on three different tasks, rare prompt-based image generation, vanishing point correction in image generation and 3D scene generation, in order to show the versatility. Our comparisons show clear improvements in alignment as well as diversity/quality of generation in all three tasks compared to the state-of-the-art approaches. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: a. We provide theoretical analysis of the impact of timestep selection strategies on diversity. b. We propose iADD, a novel training method that integrates an incremental timestep curriculum with discrete-time Feynman-Kac (FK) branching to optimally balance reward alignment and diversity. c. Extensive experiments across image and 3D scene generation demonstrate that iADD improves alignment, diversity, and rare-event success; comparisons with recent GRPO and inference-time guidance methods further show that its components are complementary to the underlying policy optimizer. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Inference-time adjustments. In order to improve alignment-diversity, reward metrics are also used solely at inference time. Such training free-approaches [ 59 , 60 , 64 ] utilize inference time measures to maximize the reward for specific generated samples. However, these techniques are also susceptible to degradation of sample quality at higher reward and moreover do not scale well during inference. Preference-based optimization. RL when used with additional preference data allows for advanced techniques that can preserve diversity. Such approaches are the counterparts of RL with Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 8 ] , popularly used in Large Language Models finetuning [ 75 ] , in the diffusion policy optimization. Methods in the category primarily follow the Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) [ 52 , 66 ] strategies either in discrete-time formulation [ 66 ] or continuous-time [ 29 ] . However, they are severely limited by the requirement of human preference data, requiring an offline strategy. Online RL for Diffusion Models. Our work is on online RL finetuning of diffusion models [ 4 , 14 , 3 , 28 , 71 , 9 ] , which has seen limited applications in diffusion models, largely due to the difficulty of the joint alignment-diversity optimization. In the topic, DDPO [ 4 ] is a seminal work that finetunes the complete trajectory as discrete steps in the Markov chain. DPOK [ 14 ] proposed a KL-divergence regularization using the DDPM formulation. Notably, [ 28 ] shows the challenges of the sparse terminal rewards [ 1 , 20 , 40 , 42 , 12 , 18 , 27 , 43 ] and suggests solely updating the later timesteps of denoising, while also incorporating contrastive pairs in branches for improving diversity. A recent work also formulates the continuous-time online RL for diffusion models [ 74 ] in the DDPM formulation while also defining each path’s value function at any given time similar to a Feynman-Kac potential. Other approaches [ 9 , 48 ] use task-specific considerations for online finetuning of diffusion models. However, current approaches do not treat time-step selection under careful theoretical considerations and under-exploit the denoising paths in reward optimization leading to poorer tradeoffs. sections.heading: Discrete-Time Diffusion Models.
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 62 ] are a class of latent variable models that learn to approximate a target data distribution by systematically reversing a predefined Markovian corruption process. Our work specifically builds upon discrete-time formulations, where the generation trajectory unfolds over a finite set of steps t ∈ { 0 , … , T } t\in\{0,\dots,T\} . Forward Process. The forward process progressively corrupts a data sample x 0 ∼ q ⁡ ( x 0 ) x_{0}\sim q(x_{0}) by injecting Gaussian noise according to a fixed variance schedule β 1 , … , β T \beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{T} . This trajectory is defined as a Markov chain: q ( x 1 : T ∣ x 0 ) = ∏ t = 1 T q ( x t ∣ x t − 1 ) , q(x_{1:T}\mid x_{0})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(x_{t}\mid x_{t-1}), (1) where the transition dynamics are given by q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x t − 1 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( x t , 1 − β t ​ x t − 1 , β t ​ I ) q(x_{t}\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}(x_{t};\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}\,x_{t-1},\beta_{t}I) . For a sufficiently large number of steps T T , the final state x T x_{T} converges to an isotropic Gaussian noise distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . Reverse Generative Process. The core objective of a diffusion model is to learn the reverse of this trajectory, constructing clean data samples starting from pure noise x T x_{T} . The reverse process is modeled as a parameterized Markov chain, often conditioned on auxiliary context c c ( e.g . , text prompts): p θ ( x 0 : T ∣ c ) = p ( x T ) ∏ t = 1 T π θ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) , p_{\theta}(x_{0:T}\mid c)=p(x_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c), (2) where π θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) \pi_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c) is approximated by a deep neural network predicting the parameters of the Gaussian transition necessary to denoise x t x_{t} into x t − 1 x_{t-1} .

sections.heading: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM)
sections.text: DDIM [ 63 ] generalizes the standard DDPM [ 23 ] forward process to a family of non-Markovian diffusion processes that share the same training objective. This decouples the number of inference steps from the number of training timesteps, enabling sampling over an arbitrary subsequence 𝒯 s ​ u ​ b ⊂ { 1 , … , T } \mathcal{T}_{sub}\subset\{1,\ldots,T\} without any retraining. Crucially, at each denoising step t t , DDIM produces an explicit estimate of the clean sample x 0 x_{0} via: x ^ 0 = x t − 1 − α t ​ ϵ θ ( t ) ​ ( x t ) α t \hat{x}_{0}=\frac{x_{t}-\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}}\,\epsilon_{\theta}^{(t)}(x_{t})}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}} (3) which we leverage to compute reward estimates from intermediate timesteps, enabling us to guide the generative trajectory before the final sample is produced.

sections.heading: Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO)
sections.text: Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO) [ 4 ] treats the iterative reverse diffusion process as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP). At each timestep t t , the state is defined as s t ≜ ( c , t , x t ) s_{t}\triangleq(c,t,x_{t}) , the action as a t ≜ x t − 1 a_{t}\triangleq x_{t-1} , and the policy is parameterized by the reverse transition probability π ⁡ ( a t ∣ s t ) ≜ π θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) \pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\triangleq\pi_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c) . The objective is to optimize a downstream reward R ⁡ ( x 0 , c ) R(x_{0},c) based on the final generated sample x 0 x_{0} and the conditioning context c c . Because each reverse transition is an isotropic Gaussian, exact per-step log-likelihoods are tractable. DDPO optimizes this MDP using an importance-weighted policy gradient estimator (DDPO-IS), allowing for multiple gradient updates using data from a previous policy parameters θ old \theta_{\text{old}} : ∇ θ ℱ ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∑ t = 0 T π θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) π θ old ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) ​ ∇ θ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , c ) ⋅ R ⁡ ( x 0 , c ) ] . \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{F}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\frac{\pi_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c)}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},c)\cdot R(x_{0},c)\right]. (4) However, standard DDPO updates all timesteps equally and relies solely on a single final reward evaluated on the complete trajectory. This sparse terminal reward and uniform credit assignment leads to reward hacking, which naturally motivates our proposed particle-based local advantage estimation and incremental training scheduling.

sections.text: The above result directly indicates that early timesteps should be updated in the RL finetuning of diffusion models, contrary to the conclusions of previous works [ 28 , 2 ] . Proposition 2 (Volume Preservation via Temporal Sparsity) Let 𝒥 T → 0 \mathcal{J}_{T\to 0} be the total Jacobian of a T T -step deterministic reverse diffusion process. For a fixed RL optimization budget, a sparse update strategy over a subset 𝒮 \mathcal{S} (where | 𝒮 | = N ≪ T |\mathcal{S}|=N\ll T ) preserves the probability volume of the prior distribution strictly better than a full update strategy ( 𝒮 = { 1 , … , T } \mathcal{S}=\{1,\dots,T\} ), as measured by the log-determinant of the global Jacobian. Remark 1 (Capacity and Over-parametrization) Proposition 2 can be interpreted through the lens of model capacity. Since distinct diffusion timesteps 𝒮 \mathcal{S} specialize in non-overlapping spectral components of the image manifold [ 13 ] , a full update strategy ( 𝒮 = { 1 , … , T } \mathcal{S}=\{1,\dots,T\} ) effectively increases the degrees of freedom available to the RL optimizer. By optimizing this over-parameterized "temporal ensemble," the model more easily finds degenerate solutions that satisfy the terminal reward R R at the cost of global prior collapse.

sections.heading: Sparse timestep update.
sections.text: The above result clearly indicates that selecting sparse timesteps for update provides strong regularization in policy optimization of the diffusion models. In fact, this also provides a tangible explanation for the improved performance of [ 28 ] when using only late timesteps with additional components of the approach. Remark 2 (Synthesis: Temporal Curriculum of Generative Reach) The relationship between generative reach (Prop. 1 ) and volume preservation (Prop. 2 ) implies an optimal curriculum for reward finetuning: an incremental expansion of the active timestep subset 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . By initially restricting optimization to a sparse set of high-leverage early timesteps ( t ∼ T t\sim T ), the model achieves global mode discovery with minimal cumulative contraction, only increasing | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| to refine local manifold details once the distribution has stabilized. Fig. 3 (B) visually illustrates the resulting sparse incremental timestep updates.

sections.heading: 4.3 Feynman-Kac Path Guidance
sections.text: An important drawback of any policy optimization strategy is the sample inefficiency due to terminal rewards obtained only at 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} . However, the Feynman-Kac theory [ 11 , 33 ] provides a way out by considering each path’s prospect at any given timestep. While previous works have used discrete-time DDIM with FK guidance for inference-time sample improvement [ 60 , 58 ] , here, we devise an approach for training.

sections.heading: Feynman–Kac (FK) view and intermediate potentials.
sections.text: Optimizing under the FK guidance requires defining a measure that evaluates a path’s reward satisfaction, termed as the potential. Following FK steering [ 59 , 60 ] , we introduce a sequence of nonnegative potentials { G t } t = 1 T \{G_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} that provide intermediate weighting of partial trajectories. Concretely, given a trajectory τ \tau , we associate the unnormalized weight w ⁡ ( τ ) = ∏ t = 1 T G t ​ ( 𝐱 t , c ) , w(\tau)\;=\;\prod_{t=1}^{T}G_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},c), (6) and define an FK-reweighted path distribution p ~ θ ​ ( τ ) ∝ p θ ​ ( τ ) ​ ∏ t = 1 T G t ​ ( 𝐱 t , c ) , \tilde{p}_{\theta}(\tau)\;\propto\;p_{\theta}(\tau)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}G_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},c), (7) where p θ ​ ( τ ) p_{\theta}(\tau) is the trajectory distribution induced by π θ \pi_{\theta} and the diffusion prior on 𝐱 T \mathbf{x}_{T} . Rather than re-evaluating a denoised prediction at every step, we use FK-style potentials to allocate compute across a branching sampling tree . Starting from an initial state 𝐱 T \mathbf{x}_{T} , we generate a set of partial trajectories by branching the reverse diffusion transitions. We then complete each branch to obtain terminal samples 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} and evaluate the terminal reward R ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , c ) R(\mathbf{x}_{0},c) . The resulting terminal rewards are used to assign a scalar potential to each branch (and, by aggregation, to its intermediate nodes), which allows us to prune branches that are unlikely to yield high reward. Fig. 3 clearly illustrates the path termination and branching for improving alignment and diversity respectively. We provide the detailed algorithm in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Image Generation.
sections.text: For image generation, we use Stable Diffusion (SD) v1.4 [ 53 ] and fine-tune only the UNet via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 25 ] for parameter-efficient adaptation, following DDPO [ 4 ] . We evaluate prompts from three image-domain categories: compositional generation (animals & actions), attribute binding (colors & fruits), and spatial relations similar to B2DiffuRL [ 28 ] . Representative prompts include “a whale riding a bike”, “brown banana”, and “a cup on tshirt”. We use the DDIM sampler [ 63 ] with settings consistent with prior RL fine-tuning work [ 28 , 4 ] ; unless otherwise stated, we use T = 20 T=20 denoising steps and classifier-free guidance scale w = 5.0 w=5.0 . The image reward is CLIPScore, i.e . , the similarity between text and image embeddings measured by CLIP [ 51 ] . The full prompt list is reported in the supplementary material. We employ an incremental training curriculum with four stages using 𝒯 sch = { 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 } \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sch}}=\{5,10,15,20\} progressively increasing the updated timesteps. We train each stage is for 10 iterations. For FK-steered sampling, we use k = 4 k=4 particles per prompt and resample every 5 denoising steps (i.e., 𝒯 res \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{res}} with period 5), with FK scale λ FK = 2.0 \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=2.0 .

sections.heading: Vanishing Point (VP) Correction.
sections.text: VP experiments use the same image-generation pipeline and sampler settings as the general synthesis task to ensure controlled comparisons. We evaluate prompts focused on long-range geometric consistency (e.g., “railway tracks” or “tunnel scenes with clear perspective cues”). We define the reward as the algebraic consensus of the straight lines converging to distinct vanishing points. We call this reward V ​ P ​ G ​ e ​ o ​ m ​ e ​ t ​ r ​ y VP\ Geometry . We detect line segments using Line Segment Detection (LSD) [ 37 ] and apply a custom line grouping algorithm. Additional algorithmic details are in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis.
sections.text: We adopt the continuous-domain variant of MiDiffusion [ 26 ] as the base diffusion model and use the 3D-FRONT dataset [ 15 ] . Following prior 3D scene-generation work [ 26 , 46 , 65 ] , each scene is represented as an unordered set of objects parameterized by semantic class, 3D position, size, and rotation. We train for 2 different rewards separately. First, we define a custom spatial reward for the prompt “a scene with a TV stand facing a bed,” which evaluates both object position and orientation. Second, we use a collision reward [ 47 ] that assigns + 1 +1 to valid scenes and otherwise applies a penalty equal to the total axis-aligned penetration depth across overlapping ground objects. Additional implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Methods Compared.
sections.text: Our primary comparison includes the pretrained reference model, DDPO [ 4 ] , its backward-progressive extension B 2 -DiffuRL [ 28 ] , and iADD; all start from the same pretrained model. We additionally evaluate recent alternatives on Template 1: inference-time Annealed Importance Guidance (AIG) [ 31 ] , DanceGRPO [ 70 ] , and BranchGRPO [ 36 ] . To test compatibility with group-relative optimization, we also replace iADD’s per-sample contrastive signal with GRPO-style groupwise advantage normalization, denoted iADD+GRPO .

sections.heading: 5.2 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Alignment–Diversity. We quantify alignment using the task-specific reward models defined in Sec. 5.1 . We measure image diversity using the Inception Score (IS), following [ 28 ] . We additionally report area-under-curve (AUC) metrics to summarize the trade-off between these objectives across operating points. Higher AUC indicates a better overall balance between alignment and diversity. For Template 1, we also report intra-prompt LPIPS: for each prompt, we generate 24 images and average all pairwise LPIPS distances. This complementary metric directly measures visual variation among samples conditioned on the same prompt.

sections.heading: 3D-Specific Metrics.
sections.text: We report Collision ( ↓ \downarrow ), using the same penetration-based formulation as the collision reward defined in Sec. 5.1 , and Class Label KL Divergence (CKL, ↓ \downarrow ). The CKL reference distribution is computed from 3D-FRONT [ 15 ] test scenes that satisfy the spatial reward constraint. To ensure a fair comparison, we evaluate all methods at a common convergence point where they reach the same mean reward threshold during training.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate models at regular intervals across 45 base prompts, generating 1,080 images per checkpoint using deterministic seeds to ensure robust measurement. To guarantee a fair comparison, we report each method at its optimal operating point—defined as the checkpoint closest to the ideal (1,1) on the Reward-Inception Score Pareto frontier.

sections.heading: Human Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate perceptual quality and prompt fidelity with a human-preference study over image Templates 1–3. Following the operating-point selection in Sec. 5.2 , we sample one image per method for each of 30 prompts and ask 40 independent raters to choose the best output in a blind comparison among the four methods (ours, B 2 -DiffuRL, DDPO, and the pretrained baseline), yielding 4,800 total judgments. sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text: Our work tackles the joint improvement of alignment, diversity, and rare-event success in diffusion models through reinforcement learning. The theoretical analysis and direct measurements of output sensitivity and Jacobian log-volume show why timestep selection must be treated carefully during reward optimization. This motivates our incremental sparse-update curriculum, while discrete Feynman–Kac pruning and branching improve the quality of the trajectories used for training. Across image generation, vanishing-point correction, and 3D scene synthesis, iADD improves the reward–diversity trade-off and rare-condition performance. Comparisons with AIG, DanceGRPO, and BranchGRPO further show that the proposed trajectory guidance and timestep curriculum remain effective beyond the original DDPO objective and can be composed with GRPO-style optimization.

sections.heading: Model Architecture.
sections.text: We use Stable Diffusion v1.4 (SDv1.4) [ 53 ] as our base model and apply LoRA [ 25 ] for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA [ 25 ] modules are injected into all attention processors across the U-Net architecture, including down-blocks, mid-blocks, and up-blocks.

sections.heading: LoRA Configuration.
sections.text: We configure LoRA [ 25 ] with rank r = 4 r=4 , alpha α = 4 \alpha=4 , and dropout p = 0.0 p=0.0 . The hidden dimensions for LoRA modules are automatically determined based on the U-Net block structure: for down-blocks and up-blocks, hidden sizes correspond to the block output channels; for mid-blocks, we use the final block output channel dimension. Cross-attention dimension is set based on whether the attention layer is self-attention (attn1) or cross-attention (attn2).

sections.heading: Training Configuration.
sections.text: We train on 20 uniformly-spaced timesteps 𝒯 train = { 1 , 51 , 101 , 151 , … , 951 } \mathcal{T}_{\text{train}}=\{1,51,101,151,\ldots,951\} from the total 1000-step diffusion schedule. We use a batch size of 16 for both training and sampling, with 16 batches per epoch. The optimizer is AdamW [ 39 ] with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and gradient accumulation over 8 steps. No learning rate scheduler is applied. Image-generation experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 machine using mixed-precision FP16 training, and we use the DDIM [ 63 ] sampler with η = 1.0 \eta=1.0 as the noise scheduler. Number of inner epochs is 2.

sections.heading: Incremental Training Schedule.
sections.text: Following our incremental training approach, we progressively expand the set of trained timesteps across 4 stages: { 5 , 10 , 15 } \{5,10,15\} timesteps, with 10 training epochs per increment.

sections.heading: FK Particle Filtering.
sections.text: For particle-based sampling, we use 4 particles per prompt. The branching timestep is set to t b = 5 t_{b}=5 , with resampling applied at timesteps { 8 , 12 , 16 } \{8,12,16\} . We use the maximum potential function with λ = 2.0 \lambda=2.0 for particle weighting.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: At inference time, we evaluate on 20 timesteps offset by 1: 𝒯 eval = { 1 , 51 , 101 , 151 , … , 951 } \mathcal{T}_{\text{eval}}=\{1,51,101,151,\ldots,951\} , following the same uniform spacing and the DDIM sampler [ 63 ] with η = 1.0 \eta=1.0 as the noise scheduler. We use classifier-free guidance scale w = 5.0 w=5.0 for inference.

sections.heading: S9.2 Vanishing Point Detection
sections.text: For vanishing point experiments, we use the same model architecture and hyperparameters as described above for image generation.

sections.heading: Base Model.
sections.text: We build upon MiDiffusion [ 26 ] , using only the continuous-domain diffusion component. The model is pretrained on bedroom scenes from the 3D-FRONT dataset [ 15 ] . Scene layouts predicted by the model are conditioned on floor plans, and we fetch corresponding CAD models from the 3D-Future [ 16 ] asset library for rendering. The model directly predicts the sample ( x 0 x_{0} ) rather than the noise.

sections.heading: Scene Representation.
sections.text: Each scene is represented as an unordered set of objects, where each object is parameterized by: • Semantic class: 22-dimensional one-hot vector (including an empty object class) • 3D position: ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) coordinates • 3D size: ( w , h , d ) (w,h,d) dimensions • 2D rotation: ( cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ ) (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) where θ \theta is the angle with the vertical axis

sections.heading: Object and Floor Plan Encoding.
sections.text: Following MiDiffusion [ 26 ] , we encode object features by processing geometric attributes through an MLP and combining them with learnable class label embeddings. For floor plan conditioning, we sample 256 boundary points from each floor plan image and compute their outward-facing normal vectors. These floor plan features are extracted using a PointNet-based [ 50 ] encoder adapted from LEGO-Net [ 67 ] .

sections.heading: Denoising Network Architecture.
sections.text: The denoising network uses a Transformer architecture with 8 layers, embedding dimension of 512, 4 attention heads, feedforward dimension of 2048, and dropout rate of 0.1. We use GELU [ 21 ] activation, adaptive layer normalization with absolute timestep encoding, and fully-connected MLP layers. The feature extractor is a PointNet-based architecture with layer dimensions [ 4 , 64 , 64 , 512 , 64 ] [4,64,64,512,64] .

sections.heading: LoRA Configuration.
sections.text: For 3D scene generation, we apply LoRA [ 25 ] to all attention projection layers (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, out_proj) in the Transformer blocks with rank r = 16 r=16 , alpha α = 16 \alpha=16 , dropout p = 0.0 p=0.0 , and no bias adaptation. This configuration provides sufficient capacity for fine-tuning while maintaining parameter efficiency.

sections.heading: Training Configuration.
sections.text: We use a batch size of 32 for both training and sampling and keep other hyperparameters same as in case of image generation. 3D scene-generation experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 2070 Ti machine using mixed-precision FP16 training.

sections.heading: FK Particle Filtering.
sections.text: Similar to image generation, we use 4 particles per prompt with the maximum potential function and λ = 2.0 \lambda=2.0 . The branching timestep is set to t b = 13 t_{b}=13 , with resampling applied at timesteps { 13 , 16 } \{13,16\} .

sections.heading: Training and Inference.
sections.text: Training and inference timesteps follow the same configuration as image generation: 20 uniformly-spaced timesteps for training and 20 offset timesteps for evaluation, using DDIM sampling with η = 1.0 \eta=1.0 . The incremental training schedule also mirrors image generation with 4 stages of { 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 } \{5,10,15,20\} timesteps and 10 epochs per increment.

sections.heading: S9.4 Branch Feynman-Kac Trajectory Rollout
sections.text: Branching [ 28 ] is applied before FK resampling to increase the number of particles from 1 to num_particles (e.g., 4). In our experiments, we branch at the 5th denoising timestep so that particles share enough early trajectory history and diverge later. This gives multiple trajectories with shared history, allowing us to select paths that produce the best and worst samples. Inference-time FK steering [ 59 ] explores different potential designs. In our experiments, max-potential and difference-potential variants achieve similar metrics. We use the following max-potential form: G t ​ ( x T , … , x t , c ) = exp ⁡ ( λ FK ​ max s = t T ⁡ R ⁡ ( x s , c ) ) G_{t}(x_{T},\ldots,x_{t},c)=\exp\!\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\max_{s=t}^{T}R(x_{s},c)\right) Max potential favors particles with higher rewards. We use this choice because [ 58 ] reports that max potential better preserves sample diversity. Similarly, prior FK-steering work studies different values of λ FK \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}} (e.g., 2 and 10). Our corresponding comparison is shown in Table S5 . Table S5 : Effect of λ FK \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}} on Inception Score. Method Inception Score Ours ( λ FK = 10 \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=10 ) 1.2830 Ours ( λ FK = 2 \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=2 ) 1.3035 FK resampling can be applied at different timesteps, but overly frequent resampling may waste computation without significant gains because particles may not have diverged enough. We therefore use resampling at the 8th, 12th, and 16th denoising timesteps. All experiments use 4 particles.

sections.heading: S9.5 Prompt Templates and Dataset
sections.text: To evaluate the effectiveness and generalization capabilities of our method, we curated a diverse set of prompt templates spanning several semantic and structural categories. These templates are designed to test the model’s ability to handle compositional generalization, out-of-distribution (OOD) attribute binding, spatial reasoning, and geometric regularity.

sections.heading: Prompt Templates
sections.text: We utilize four distinct templates [ 28 ] , each targeting a specific challenge in text-to-image generation: • Template 1: Animal-Action Compositionality. This template pairs various animals (e.g., cat, shark, kangaroo ) with specific actions (e.g., riding a bike, playing chess, washing dishes ). The dataset contains 45 prompts. • Template 2: Rare Color-Object Binding. This template focuses on binding colors to fruits and vegetables. We define Common prompts as those following natural distributions (e.g., red apple, yellow banana ) and Rare prompts as unnatural or OOD combinations (e.g., brown banana, green strawberry ). Total 40 prompts are present for this template. • Template 3: Spatial Relations. This template evaluates spatial reasoning using relations such as on, under, on the left of and on the right of . It contains total of 40 spatial composition prompts to test the model’s adherence to relational constraints. • Template 4: Geometric Structures. Designed specifically for evaluating the Vanishing Point reward, this template includes 24 prompts describing scenes with strong linear perspective, such as railroad tracks stretching to the horizon or an empty straight road disappearing into the distance .

sections.heading: S16 Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: A primary limitation of our approach is its higher training cost. As reported in Table S11 , our method requires 7.43 GPU hours, compared with 2.55 GPU hours for DDPO, to reach the same mean reward (CLIP score of 0.388). This overhead is mainly attributable to the Feynman-Kac particle-based sampling procedure, which requires repeated reward evaluations during trajectory generation. Although the incremental timestep update strategy partially reduces this cost, overall training remains slower than DDPO. Importantly, after training, inference-time cost is comparable to DDPO [ 4 ] and does not incur the additional overhead associated with inference-time FK steering [ 59 ] . A second limitation concerns reward estimation from noisy intermediate states. Our current approach computes rewards from denoised predictions inferred directly from noisy latents, which can be unreliable at earlier timesteps. For instance, in 3D indoor scene layout generation, improvements are limited because critical geometric attributes (e.g., object size and position) are often not accurately recoverable from noisy states, even midway through the denoising trajectory. In such settings, alternative reward-estimation schemes, as discussed in inference-time FK steering [ 59 ] , may be more suitable. Future work should investigate more accurate estimators of terminal rewards from intermediate noisy states. In addition, stronger reward models are needed to improve prompt-image alignment. The CLIP [ 51 ] score used in our experiments has known failure modes; for example, for the prompt "chicken playing chess", it may assign a high score to images showing cooked chicken near a chessboard, despite weak semantic alignment. A natural next step is to extend this framework to video diffusion models, where physics-aware rewards from simulation engines could encourage temporally consistent and physically plausible video generation.

sections.heading: S17 Broader Impacts.
sections.text: Diffusion-based generative models are increasingly used in design, education, media creation, simulation, and human–AI interaction. A key practical limitation, however, is that high-scoring outputs do not necessarily satisfy physical or geometric rules of the real world. Our work shows that reinforcement-learning-based alignment can be trained to better respect task-specific constraints (e.g., perspective consistency or collision-free 3D layouts) while preserving output quality. This may improve reliability in applications where structural correctness matters. At the same time, more controllable generation can also be misused to produce convincing but misleading synthetic content. For this reason, safeguards, responsible deployment, and robust detection and auditing tools remain essential.

However, current approaches to reward optimizations do so at the cost of diversity and quality. In this paper, we provide better tradeoffs through careful theoretical considerations and method design. We analyze the theoretical framework and mathematically demonstrate that only-latter timestep updates of diffusion model may be harmful for diversity contrary to the conclusions presented in a previous work. Additionally, we propose an incremental Feynman-Kac training based on strong theoretical foundations in order to achieve the best-yet alignment-diversity tradeoffs. We perform extensive experiments and compare our method against related diffusion policy optimization approaches in three different tasks and also provide strong ablations for each component, thus validating strong performance gains in both alignment and diversity. (a) Our method, iADD, achieves a higher CLIP Score at any given diversity level compared to other methods. Notably, as reward increases, competing methods (DDPO and B 2 B^{2} -DiffuRL) produce increasingly cartoonish, over-saturated outputs, whereas our method preserves photorealistic quality throughout training. Rare prompts represent conditions that inherently yield low-reward outcomes under the pretrained model. 1 Introduction Diffusion Models are currently the gold standard for generation and editing tasks on images [ 23 , 63 , 38 , 53 , 64 , 62 , 44 , 54 ] , videos [ 24 , 22 , 5 ] as well as 3D scenes [ 17 , 26 , 65 ] or objects. Through time-dependent iterative movement defining a path, diffusion methods learn to reach the target data distribution, exhibiting strong generalization and diversity [ 13 , 35 , 44 ] . Nevertheless, the quality of the modeling is limited by the target distribution samples; thus in most cases generation quality is naturally impacted for rare classes and specific user constraints. Reinforcement Learning (RL) [ 68 , 56 , 45 , 55 ] has the potential to address the problem, without using additional data, in the ideals of learning solely through experience [ 57 ] . Recent works [ 4 , 14 , 74 , 28 , 49 , 72 , 69 ] have precisely addressed the problem of finetuning the reverse diffusion process online, by applying the RL algorithm [ 68 ] . However, naive policy optimization of diffusion models can lead to mode collapse and general quality degradation of the generated samples [ 14 , 28 ] . This is reflected in the alignment-diversity tradeoffs , see Fig. 1 . Circumventing mode collapse and general quality degradation in lack of additional preference data [ 66 , 34 , 73 , 32 ] , though important is highly challenging. Thus, most approaches tend to be domain specific, and thus are validated on specific tasks. A more generic and theoretically grounded study of the alignment-diversity tradeoffs under the constraints of additional preference data-free rewards, remains under-explored. Existing solutions often perform regularization, e.g . through selected timestep updates [ 2 , 28 ] or via measuring the KL divergence [ 14 ] . Specifically, [ 28 ] intuitively argues that reward backpropagation is more reliable for latter timesteps and thus do not update the model on earlier timesteps. On the other hand, [ 2 , 41 ] refine middle timesteps based on the observation of how semantics are constructed in diffusion models [ 13 , 7 ] . Similarly, [ 14 , 74 ] specifically consider the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) in order to propose reward optimization strategies. Furthermore, [ 74 ] proposes a continuous time formulation in DDPM for RL policy optimization. In this paper, we study the alignment-diversity tradeoff in finetuning discrete-time denoising diffusion model through early intervention as well as careful regularization. We formulate the tradeoff problem as that of attaining the minimum change in the target samples required for the alignment, while preserving the original diversity through structural regularization, and target distribution’s volume preservation. We discover that attaining higher alignment with minimal diversity tradeoff requires early intervention via two processes. The first and retrospectively obvious solution is to update the early timesteps of the reverse denoising path, contrary to [ 28 ] that updates the late timesteps. We provide actionable theoretical results that untangles the puzzle of timestep selection. The results justify partial timestep selection from the viewpoint of target distribution’s volume preservation. Moreover, the theoretical analyses suggest an approach, which incrementally increases the per-iteration sparse timestep updates, over the course of the finetuning. Additionally, our second solution is to perform early intervention by looking ahead in the denoising path. Specifically, we propose the discrete-time implementation of the Feynman-Kac path guidance [ 11 , 33 , 58 , 60 , 61 , 30 ] during training in the following two ways: discontinuing least promising paths with low reward expectations to improve the alignment and branching the promising ones in order to encourage diversity. Table 1 shows the relative impact and relevant theory behind the method’s components. Figure 2 : Versatility across diverse generation tasks. Our final method, termed, iADD thus employs both early timestep update, early intervention as well as structural regularization in order to obtain a balanced approach to reward-based finetuning of diffusion models. We perform experiments on three different tasks, rare prompt-based image generation, vanishing point correction in image generation and 3D scene generation, in order to show the versatility. Our comparisons show clear improvements in alignment as well as diversity/quality of generation in all three tasks compared to the state-of-the-art approaches. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: a. We provide theoretical analysis of the impact of timestep selection strategies on diversity. b. We propose iADD, a novel training method that integrates an incremental timestep curriculum with discrete-time Feynman-Kac (FK) branching to optimally balance reward alignment and diversity. c. Extensive experiments across image and 3D scene generation demonstrate that iADD improves alignment, diversity, and rare-event success; comparisons with recent GRPO and inference-time guidance methods further show that its components are complementary to the underlying policy optimizer. In order to improve alignment-diversity, reward metrics are also used solely at inference time. Such training free-approaches [ 59 , 60 , 64 ] utilize inference time measures to maximize the reward for specific generated samples. However, these techniques are also susceptible to degradation of sample quality at higher reward and moreover do not scale well during inference. Preference-based optimization. RL when used with additional preference data allows for advanced techniques that can preserve diversity. Such approaches are the counterparts of RL with Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 8 ] , popularly used in Large Language Models finetuning [ 75 ] , in the diffusion policy optimization. Methods in the category primarily follow the Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) [ 52 , 66 ] strategies either in discrete-time formulation [ 66 ] or continuous-time [ 29 ] . However, they are severely limited by the requirement of human preference data, requiring an offline strategy. Online RL for Diffusion Models. Our work is on online RL finetuning of diffusion models [ 4 , 14 , 3 , 28 , 71 , 9 ] , which has seen limited applications in diffusion models, largely due to the difficulty of the joint alignment-diversity optimization. In the topic, DDPO [ 4 ] is a seminal work that finetunes the complete trajectory as discrete steps in the Markov chain. A recent work also formulates the continuous-time online RL for diffusion models [ 74 ] in the DDPM formulation while also defining each path’s value function at any given time similar to a Feynman-Kac potential. Other approaches [ 9 , 48 ] use task-specific considerations for online finetuning of diffusion models. However, current approaches do not treat time-step selection under careful theoretical considerations and under-exploit the denoising paths in reward optimization leading to poorer tradeoffs.
